title: From a Unit Cell to a Protective Structure: A Short Review of Energy-Absorbing Cellular Metamaterials
content: Cellular metamaterials are changing the way protective structures are designed. Instead of relying on conventional foams and honeycombs, engineers can now architect lightweight lattices whose collapse sequence, transmitted force and energy absorption are set by geometry. This short review summarises recent progress in cellular metamaterials for impact, crash and blast protection. Positive, negative (auxetic) and zero Poisson's ratio topologies are first compared in terms of their deformation mechanisms and the usual crashworthiness indicators. Design strategies are then discussed, including functional grading, hybrid auxetic–non-auxetic cells, hierarchical and fractal architectures, bio-inspired concepts, topology optimisation and data-driven inverse design. Fabrication by additive manufacturing and by simpler sheet-based routes, together with quasi-static, drop-weight, high-strain-rate and blast testing, is reviewed next. Particular attention is given to multifunctional metamaterials and to modular, multistable and 4D-printed designs whose response can be tuned or restored after fabrication. Applications such as blast-resistant gates, sandwich panels, steel columns and anti-ram bollards are used to show how these concepts reach practice. The review closes with open challenges, notably scale-up, consistent reporting of performance indicators, validation of data-driven models under dynamic loading and the extension of reprogrammable designs to high-energy protective applications.
